title: Budshah Recalls the Exiles
subtitle: Budshah’s Great Return: Law, Memory and the Healing of Kashmir
era: Reversal edicts and religious settlement, c. 1420s-1430s CE
region: Srinagar, Naushahr and the returning routes from Punjab
moral: A just ruler repairs wounds without pretending they never happened.

sources.note: Primary account of exile recall, Brahmin patronage and Budshah's Sanskrit court.
Records temple repair at Naushahr and permission for rebuilding and personal law.

sources.citation: R.C. Majumdar, History and Culture of the Indian People, Vol. VI; Hasan, Kashmir Under the Sultans
sources.note: Modern synthesis of jizya abolition, stipends and tax relief.

panels.shot: epic mid-shot of a lone sovereign on a terrace overlooking Srinagar valley

dialogue.text: In a Kashmir scarred by exile and tax, Sultan Zain-ul-Abidin—Budshah—must choose: keep his father’s hard law, or recall the banished and restore temples to life.

panels.shot: slow push-in on contemplative ruler seated indoors

dialogue.text: Years after seizing the throne, Budshah sits between two scripts—Persian orders and Sanskrit chronicles—and feels the weight of a divided kingdom upon his shoulders.
Jonaraja’s verses speak of an earlier time, when fear and harsh edicts drove many Hindus from the valley towards Punjab and beyond, leaving shrines untended and homes abandoned.

panels.shot: close, somber interior of ruined temple

dialogue.text: Srivara later records temples at Naushahr left to decay, their idols and halls neglected as the kingdom turned its gaze elsewhere and fear hardened into policy.

panels.shot: low-angle throne room with advisors in shadow

dialogue.text: Now the young Sultan faces a test: keep the jizya and heavy levies that mark his father’s reign, or loosen them and risk the anger of those who profit by fear.

dialogue.speaker: zain_ul_abidin
dialogue.text: A kingdom built on fear cannot endure. The jizya shall be abolished.
Chronicles and modern historians agree: Budshah ends the jizya, the poll tax on his Hindu subjects, and offers tax relief that softens the hard edge of statute.
Jonaraja notes how Budshah recalls learned Brahmins to court, grants them stipends again, and allows Dharmashastra to govern their personal law within the wider sultanate.
By commissioning Jonaraja to continue Kalhana’s Rajatarangini, Budshah pulls Sanskrit memory back into the centre of power, letting Kashmir’s past be sung in its old tongue.

panels.shot: dynamic riding shot on mountain road

dialogue.text: Yet the story is not only of law within the valley. Jonaraja describes royal messengers and orders sent along these routes, urging exiles in Punjab and beyond to return home.

panels.shot: soft-focus scene of exiles hearing news

dialogue.text: Word spreads among displaced families: the Budshah has changed the law, abolished jizya, and invites those who fled to come back without fear or payment.

panels.shot: wide shot of caravan approaching valley

dialogue.text: Caravans move again, this time towards Kashmir. The return is not a reversal of all that changed, but a legal promise: no new coercion, room for old customs to breathe.

dialogue.speaker: zain_ul_abidin
dialogue.text: This valley is yours as it is mine. Return, rebuild, remember.

panels.shot: reverent interior shot of temple repair

dialogue.text: Srivara describes Budshah allowing temple rebuilding, even ordering repairs at Naushahr. Worship sites once neglected slowly rise again under the Sultan’s protection.

panels.shot: balanced street-level shot showing mixed community

dialogue.text: The Muslim community remains, the sultanate endures. Budshah does not erase social change; he instead dismantles the state’s harshest tools and lets difference exist under a more even law.
Modern scholars see in this moment both broad tolerance and a careful re-legitimation of Sanskrit elites, woven into an Islamic sultanate without undoing its foundations.

panels.shot: gentle close-up of aged ruler at window

dialogue.text: Budshah’s legacy survives in chronicles that praise his policies, and in memories of a time when a ruler chose to repair wounds without denying the scars that remained.
